before:
Ulysses follows Leopold Bloom, a thirty-eight-year-old Jewish advertising canvasser, through one day in Dublin: Thursday, June 16, 1904. He fries a kidney for breakfast, buys soap, attends a funeral, places a newspaper ad, eats a Gorgonzola sandwich, watches a young woman on a beach, drinks in a maternity hospital, hallucinates in a brothel, walks home with a younger man, makes cocoa in his kitchen, and gets into bed beside his wife at two in the morning. Around him is Stephen Dedalus, a twenty-two-year-old failed poet still in mourning for his mother, who drifts across Bloom's path five times before they finally meet near midnight. The book closes with Bloom's wife Molly, alone in bed and awake, in a forty-five-page unpunctuated monologue that ends with the most-quoted "yes" in literature.

Joyce wrote Ulysses between 1914 and 1921, in Trieste, Zurich, and Paris. He published it in 1922 in Paris because no Anglophone publisher would touch it; it was banned for obscenity in the United States until 1934 and in the United Kingdom until 1936. The novel maps onto Homer's Odyssey episode by episode — Bloom is Odysseus, Stephen is Telemachus, Molly is Penelope — and Joyce gave each of its eighteen episodes a distinct hour, location, organ of the body, and prose technique.

Ulysses is the founding work of literary modernism and the most ambitious novel in English. It contains interior monologue, newspaper headlines, parodies of every prose style from Anglo-Saxon to Victorian magazine, a chapter in catechism, a chapter staged as a play. The technical detail of Dublin is so exact that Joyce claimed the city could be reconstructed from his book if it were destroyed. The novel's argument is that consciousness — ordinary, drifting, sexual, hungry, grieving consciousness — is the proper subject of fiction, and that an ad salesman's Thursday is as worth attending to as any king's homecoming.
after:
On Thursday, June 16, 1904, Leopold Bloom fries himself a kidney for breakfast in Dublin. He sells newspaper advertising. His day takes him to a funeral, a newspaper office and Davy Byrne's pub for a Gorgonzola sandwich. Elsewhere in the city, young Stephen Dedalus teaches a history lesson and grieves for his mother. The two men walk together late that night, and Bloom makes cocoa in his kitchen. The book closes with Molly Bloom lying awake beside her husband.

Joyce wrote Ulysses between 1914 and 1921, in Trieste, Zurich, and Paris. Sylvia Beach published it in Paris in 1922. An American court ruling in 1933 cleared the way for the authorised US edition in 1934; the first British edition appeared in 1936. The novel maps onto Homer's Odyssey episode by episode — Bloom is Odysseus, Stephen is Telemachus, Molly is Penelope — and Joyce developed schemes linking its eighteen episodes with locations, times, bodily organs and narrative techniques; not every category applies to every episode.

Ulysses is a major work of literary modernism and an unusually ambitious experiment in the English-language novel. It contains interior monologue, newspaper headlines, parodies of prose styles from Anglo-Saxon to Victorian magazine, a chapter in catechism, a chapter staged as a play. The technical detail of Dublin is so exact that Joyce claimed the city could be reconstructed from his book if it were destroyed. The novel's argument is that consciousness — ordinary, drifting, sexual, hungry, grieving consciousness — is the proper subject of fiction, and that an ad salesman's Thursday is as worth attending to as any king's homecoming.

before: A thirty-eight-year-old Dublin advertising canvasser of Hungarian-Jewish descent. His son Rudy died at eleven days old, eleven years before the novel opens, and he and his wife Molly have not slept together fully since. He is curious, kind, scientifically minded, mildly cuckolded, and quietly grieving. He likes inner organs of beasts and fowls. He carries a potato in his pocket. The novel follows his consciousness for most of fourteen hours and finds, in the texture of one ordinary man's attention, a hero Homer could not have imagined.
after: A thirty-eight-year-old Dublin advertising canvasser of Hungarian-Jewish descent. His son Rudy died at eleven days old, just over ten years before the novel opens, and he and his wife Molly have not had full sexual intercourse for more than ten years. He is curious, kind, scientifically minded, aware of his wife’s affair, and quietly grieving. He likes inner organs of beasts and fowls. He carries a potato in his pocket. The novel follows his consciousness through much of the day and into the night and finds, in the texture of one ordinary man's attention, a hero Homer could not have imagined.

before: A twenty-two-year-old schoolteacher, occasional poet, and former seminarian, returned from a year in Paris when his mother fell ill and refused to pray at her deathbed. The novel inherits him from Joyce's earlier book A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. He is brilliant, proud, articulate, broke, and spiritually homeless. He is Telemachus looking for a father he cannot quite name, and his own actual father — the drunken, sentimental Simon Dedalus — is everywhere in the city he is trying to leave.

He is brilliant, proud, articulate, broke, and spiritually homeless. before: Born Marion Tweedy in Gibraltar to a Spanish-Jewish mother and an Irish father, now a thirty-three-year-old professional singer in Dublin. She has spent the afternoon in bed with her concert promoter Blazes Boylan. She is sensual, sharp, funny, and intelligent in a way most of the men in the book do not register. Her closing monologue — eight unpunctuated sentences across forty-five pages, drifting through memory, lust, marriage, and the line between them — is the most famous passage in modernist fiction and the novel's last word on what consciousness is.

before: A medical student who shares the Martello tower at Sandycove with Stephen and an English visitor. Mulligan opens the novel intoning a Latin parody of the Mass while shaving on the parapet. He is brilliant, mocking, bawdy, and corrosive — a wit who uses comedy as a way of refusing to take anything seriously, including grief. He has called Stephen's mother "beastly dead." Stephen will not forgive him. Joyce based him on his real-life friend and rival Oliver St. John Gogarty.

before: A Dublin man-about-town, concert promoter, and Molly's lover. Bloom knows the affair is happening; he knows Boylan has an appointment at his house at four o'clock; he watches a clock cross four o'clock and keeps walking. Boylan appears physically only briefly — picking up a basket of fruit on Grafton Street, riding a hansom — but his presence shadows every scene Bloom navigates between morning and night. He is what Bloom is not: confident, unreflective, sexually direct, and uninteresting on the inside.

before: Joyce divided Ulysses into eighteen episodes and wrote each in a different prose register. The first three are relatively conventional interior monologue, easing the reader in. After that, the techniques start coming apart on purpose. The Aeolus chapter is broken up by newspaper headlines and editorial parodies. The Oxen of the Sun episode runs the entire history of English prose styles in chronological pastiche, from Anglo-Saxon alliterative verse through Bunyan and Sterne to a contemporary American religious tract. Circe is staged as a hallucinatory play with stage directions and impossible scene changes. Ithaca is written entirely in catechism — question and answer — describing Bloom's kitchen down to the volume of water in his teakettle and the trajectory of his urination. The form is the argument. A single ordinary day in a single city contains every register a writer could use, and no single register is enough. Every later novel that mixes techniques across its chapters is in this novel's debt.
after: Joyce divided Ulysses into eighteen episodes and wrote each in a different prose register. The first three move between external narration and Stephen’s thoughts; the third, Proteus, is already demanding. After that, the techniques start coming apart on purpose. The Aeolus chapter is broken up by newspaper headlines and editorial parodies. The Oxen of the Sun episode runs a succession of English prose styles in chronological pastiche, from Anglo-Saxon alliterative verse through Bunyan and Sterne to a contemporary American religious tract. Circe is staged as a hallucinatory play with stage directions and impossible scene changes. Ithaca is written entirely in catechism — question and answer — describing Bloom's kitchen down to the volume of water in his teakettle and the trajectory of his urination. The form is the argument. A single ordinary day in a single city contains every register a writer could use, and no single register is enough. Its shifts of technique have become an influential model for later fiction.

before: Homer's Odysseus is a king, a warrior, a survivor of the Trojan War who washes up on Phaeacian shores naked and is recognized for who he is. Joyce's Odysseus is an ad salesman whose wife is sleeping with another man, who buys a bar of lemon soap and forgets to pay for it, who eats a Gorgonzola sandwich alone in Davy Byrne's pub, who masturbates on Sandymount Strand watching a stranger during a fireworks display, who walks home in the small hours and lets a young drunk poet he has just met sleep in his kitchen. Joyce's argument is that the patterns Homer found in heroic life — wandering, return, recognition, the offer of food to a stranger, the long delay before a husband and wife actually see each other again — are present in any sufficiently attentive Thursday in any sufficiently attended-to city. Most modern fiction has worked from this premise since. The premise is the modern novel's permission to take seriously the lives that epic could not.
after: Homer's Odysseus is a king, a warrior, a survivor of the Trojan War who washes up on Phaeacian shores naked and is recognized for who he is. Joyce's Odysseus is an ad salesman whose wife is sleeping with another man, who takes a bar of lemon soap with a promise to pay later, who eats a Gorgonzola sandwich alone in Davy Byrne's pub, who masturbates on Sandymount Strand watching a stranger during a fireworks display, who walks home in the small hours and offers the young poet a bed for the night. Stephen declines. Joyce's argument is that the patterns Homer found in heroic life — wandering, return, recognition, the offer of food to a stranger, the long delay before a husband and wife actually see each other again — are present in any sufficiently attentive Thursday in any sufficiently attended-to city. That attention to ordinary experience has helped shape later fiction.

before: Molly Bloom's closing chapter — episode eighteen, called Penelope — runs forty-five pages in eight long sentences with almost no punctuation, almost no paragraph breaks, and almost no concession to the conventional reader. She is alone in bed in the small hours, drifting between memory and immediate physical sensation, working through her marriage, her lover that afternoon, her dead infant son, her childhood in Gibraltar, her sense of her own body and what it has been, her tenderness for her husband she rarely shows him, and finally the single afternoon on Howth Head years earlier when Bloom proposed and she said yes. The technique is Joyce's purest version of stream of consciousness, and the chapter ends — "yes I said yes I will Yes" — with the most-quoted affirmation in English-language fiction. Reading it is encountering the book's argument that consciousness is not what novels had assumed it was: not orderly, not single-tracked, not in sentences, not divisible into thought and sensation, but a continuous drift the prose has to invent a new technique to follow.
